column1: # Every loopback port this campaign has already bound, so "a port that has never
# been used" stops being something anyone has to remember.
# The rule this file exists to enforce: a run gets ports no earlier run had. Reusing
# one is not forbidden, but it must be DELIBERATE and it must be SAID — a report
# calling a reused port "new" is the failure this ledger prevents. `run_controlled.sh`
# refuses a port listed here unless --allow-reused-ports is passed, and every run
# records, per port, whether it was a first use or a reuse.
# Read the scope honestly: this ledger records what is KNOWN, and it was written
# after the fact. Absence from it is not proof a port was never bound on odb24 by
# anything — it means no run of THIS campaign recorded binding it. Production's own
# ports are listed because they are the ones that must never be touched at all.
# A port allocated to a run that never started is listed too, and said to be so.
# It was never bound, so it is not "used" in the sense the host would report — but
# a run's evidence is named against the ports it was launched with, and proposing
# one of them again as fresh is the same mistake in a quieter form.
# TWO STATES THAT ARE NOT THE SAME THING, and this file used to write both as "SPENT".
#   the RUN's identity   — CONSUMED once a run has been authorised and started, whether
#                          or not it reached the point of binding anything. A consumed
#                          identity (label, staging path, workdir, app name) is never
#                          reused, because its evidence is named against it.
#   the PORT's history   — either BOUND (a socket really listened on it) or
#                          NEVER BOUND (allocated to a run that stopped first).
# A port can be retired without ever having been bound, and saying "SPENT" for both
# loses the difference: a reader cannot tell whether a listener ever existed, which is
# exactly what they came to this file to find out. The vocabulary from here on:
#   BOUND / SPENT           a socket listened on it; it is retired
#   RETIRED-NEVER-BOUND     allocated to a consumed identity; NO socket ever listened
#   allocated, not yet run  proposed by a request; nothing has happened yet
# Rows written before this note use the older, conflated wording. They are LEFT AS THEY
# ARE: their prose already says whether a port was bound, and rewriting historical
# evidence to match a newer vocabulary is not a correction, it is an edit to the record.
# Maintained by hand and by commit. The runners cannot append to it: they execute
# from a throwaway export, so anything they wrote would be discarded with it. Adding
# the ports of a completed run is a deliberate edit before the next one is proposed.
# RETIRED-NEVER-BOUND, and deliberately NOT listed as port rows: c1i (18321/18322/18969),
# (19071/19072/19079), and c1q's proposed 19101/19102/19103. run_controlled.sh refuses a
# port this file names, and reads it from the export of the subject it runs, so a port
# recorded before its run is a port that run cannot use. c1i never started; c1j aborted at
# connection identity; c1k at the shared-environment stage; c1m at uv resolution; c1n at
# production identity. None of them ever bound a socket. c1p DID bind its three and they are listed below as SPENT. c1q's are added only after it runs.
# The c1m..c1p ports sit OUTSIDE 18241-18999 deliberately: test_staging_launcher.sh scans
# that range for a free port, so a run port inside it is ambiguous even though the scan
# allocates nothing. 19061 and 19081 were also rejected -- each appears as a coincidental
# substring inside a uv.lock URL, and "named nowhere else" should mean exactly that.
# port
